title: Whittled pine butter spreader
subtitle: A thin-bladed spreader for soft butter and soft cheese
excerpt: A pine butter spreader: 18 cm overall, a 7 cm blade that is flat on one face and gently convex on the other, and a turned-taper handle. Seasoned pine, knife only, danish-oil finish. A knife-only project suited to an hour of evening practice.
sourceNotes: Scandinavian sloyd tradition knife-only exercises from Uno Cygnaeus's 1866 school programme; adapted for pine over basswood.

glossaryTerms.definition: Air-dried or kiln-dried wood at a stable moisture content for indoor use (8 to 12 per cent). Does not shrink after working.
A short straight-bladed knife with a stout handle; the Swedish school-craft standard for whittling and spoon-carving.

content.text: A butter spreader is a flat-bladed knife shape with no cutting edge: blunt on both sides, thin in the blade, and comfortable in the hand. At 18 cm overall, it rests across the rim of a butter dish without sliding in. This project uses
seasoned wood
pine from a length of standard softwood board. Beginner level, knife only, one evening's work.
Before you start cutting.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one. The dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.
Wood
Pine from a standard softwood board (19 mm PAR),
seasoned

and stable. Pine carves fast under the sloyd knife and requires less edge sharpness than hardwoods, which makes it ideal for practising knife grip and cut control. The resin in pine is not food-safe in contact with oily or wet foods over long periods, so this spreader should be used for dry bread and hard cheese, and finished with danish oil rather than a food-contact oil. A 20 cm length sawn from the board is the starting blank.
Tools
Sloyd knife: all shaping.
Leather strop: strop every fifteen minutes.
Danish oil: a durable, penetrating finish for utility pieces.
Method
Step 1: Mark the blank

Draw the spreader on the wide face of the board section. The blade is 7 cm long, 3 cm wide at the shoulder, tapering to 2 cm at the tip. The handle is 11 cm long, 2.5 cm wide at the shoulder, 1.8 cm at the end. The silhouette is all on one plane at this stage.
Step 2: Cut the plan outline
Use push cuts with the
sloyd knife
to remove the waste outside the drawn lines. Pine removes quickly: long, controlled strokes on the straight sections, thumb-pivot cuts on the curves.
Step 3: Thin the blade

The blade starts at 19 mm thick. Reduce it to 4 mm at the tip, 6 mm at the shoulder. Work from both faces, taking alternating passes. The flat face of the spreader is held against the cutting board at this angle: tilt the blank and use push cuts to thin the blade edge, keeping the flat face flat and only removing material from the convex face.
Step 4: Round the handle

Reduce the handle from a rectangular cross-section to an oval. Eight-sided first: a push cut along each of the four corners. Then take the eight edges to sixteen, then round the sixteen to a smooth oval. This is the classic Scandinavian sloyd exercise that builds the knife control needed for every subsequent whittling project.
Step 5: Blend the shoulder

The shoulder is where the oval handle meets the flat blade. Use short push cuts to blend the transition so there is no abrupt step. The shoulder on a spreader is wider than the blade on both sides; pare the excess from the blade side inward rather than from the handle side outward to keep the blade flat.
Finishing

Apply danish oil with a cloth. Pine absorbs the first coat fast. Leave ten minutes, apply a second coat, leave thirty minutes, wipe the surplus. Leave overnight before a third coat the next day. Danish oil hardens to a durable film in five to seven days. The spreader is usable on dry food after the cure.
Variations
Make four from a single board section and give them as a set with a soft-cheese board.
Burn initials into the handle end with a pyrography pen before finishing.
The same blank shape cut from cherry or maple with raw-linseed finish becomes a food-contact-safe honey spreader.

attrs.cause: A knot in the pine blank caused the cut to deviate into short grain.
attrs.fix: Select pine blanks without knots in the blade section. In the handle, knots are cosmetically acceptable.

attrs.symptom: The handle is not truly oval, it has flat spots
attrs.cause: The eight-to-sixteen step was skipped or rushed.
attrs.fix: Go back to a well-defined eight-sided cross-section and work from there. Do not try to round over flat spots in one cut.
